title: MCP vs REST for Agent Tools: Protocol and Integration Tradeoffs
excerpt: Compare MCP and REST for agent tools through discovery, lifecycle, authorization, compatibility, and a hypothetical inventory-reservation integration.
content:
MCP and REST solve different parts of an agent integration. REST commonly describes a resource-oriented application interface over HTTP. MCP defines how an AI host and a capability server exchange protocol messages, discover supported features, and invoke tools. An MCP server can call an existing HTTP API; adopting MCP does not require replacing the underlying service.

The useful architecture decision is where interoperability earns its operational cost. This guide develops a hypothetical inventory assistant and separates protocol facts from proposed integration choices. The MCP references use the explicit 2025-11-25 specification version, rather than assuming every deployed client supports the same feature set.

## Compare the integration layers before comparing products

MCP organizes an integration around a host, client connections, and servers exposing capabilities. The host coordinates the model and permissions; individual clients communicate with servers. Resources, prompts, and tools are distinct protocol primitives. This architecture provides a shared integration vocabulary, but its boundaries still need enforcement in the actual implementation. [MCP architecture specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/architecture).

For our proposed inventory assistant, the business service already owns products, stock reservations, and fulfillment rules. A direct agent adapter could call its HTTP endpoints. Alternatively, an MCP server could expose inventory capabilities while calling those same endpoints behind the boundary.

The business invariants should remain identical in both designs. A reservation cannot exceed available stock, an actor cannot reserve inventory for another tenant, and a timed-out reservation needs reconciliation. Moving these rules into model instructions would weaken either architecture.

Also separate REST from HTTP itself. An application may use JSON over HTTP without following a particular REST design rigorously. MCP over an HTTP transport also uses HTTP infrastructure. Consequently, “MCP versus HTTP” is usually the wrong comparison; identify the application contract and the additional protocol behavior being evaluated.

## Discovery is useful only when the catalog has meaning

The versioned MCP tool specification defines `tools/list` for discovering tool metadata and `tools/call` for invocation. Tool definitions include input schemas and may declare output schemas. Discovery does not determine whether a model should use a capability for a particular customer's request. [MCP tools specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools).

In the hypothetical assistant, a useful catalog might expose `inventory_find_product`, `inventory_check_availability`, and `inventory_create_reservation`. These names describe business actions. Automatically converting every internal endpoint into a tool could expose administrative operations, obsolete routes, or implementation details irrelevant to the task.

Direct HTTP integration can also be described systematically. OpenAPI defines a machine-readable interface description for HTTP APIs, including operations and schemas. Thus, MCP does not have exclusive ownership of discoverable or typed interfaces. The meaningful difference is the interaction contract expected by the consuming hosts. [OpenAPI specification 3.1.1](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.1.html).

Our design recommendation is to maintain a deliberately curated agent catalog regardless of the transport. Include when to use a capability, required evidence, authority requirements, and meaningful result states. Do not confuse a discoverable operation with an operation that should be available to every session.

## Budget for lifecycle and compatibility work

MCP initialization negotiates protocol compatibility and capabilities before normal operation. The client starts with `initialize`, and successful setup is followed by an initialized notification. Optional features must be supported by the relevant participants rather than inferred from the existence of a connection. [MCP lifecycle specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle).

This introduces an integration state machine alongside the business workflow. In our proposed deployment, track whether the connection is initializing, usable, reconnecting, or unavailable. Do not dispatch a reservation through a connection whose negotiation failed. Record the selected protocol version and supported capabilities in diagnostic data.

A direct adapter has compatibility work too: API versions, authentication changes, schemas, and error semantics can evolve. Its lifecycle may be simpler when a single controlled application calls a small stable service. MCP can become more attractive when several compatible hosts would otherwise require separate integration adapters.

Treat compatibility as a tested matrix. A server passing its own unit tests does not establish that every host correctly handles its structured results or optional capabilities. Test the actual client versions and configurations the product supports.

## Keep authorization distinct from tool descriptions

The referenced MCP authorization specification addresses HTTP-based transports and defines OAuth-related discovery and token requirements when authorization is implemented. It distinguishes that flow from credential handling for stdio integrations. In particular, audience binding and privilege restriction remain security concerns; a generic connection is not unlimited authority. [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization).

For the inventory example, establish actor and tenant identity outside model-generated arguments. The reservation service should enforce those values at execution. A tool description saying “only reserve your own stock” cannot replace authorization checks.

If an MCP server calls a downstream API, define which identity it uses and how delegated rights are constrained. Avoid treating a token issued for the MCP resource as a token that can automatically be forwarded to an unrelated service. An adapter may need a separate downstream credential and an explicit mapping between the authorized user and allowed operations.

The same principle applies to direct adapters: a model should not receive a broad administrator token merely because the integration is internal. [Least-privilege agent tools](/blog/least-privilege-agent-tools) develops the capability and credential boundaries in more detail.

## Walk through a hypothetical reservation request

Assume a warehouse operator asks the assistant to reserve three units of a specific part for an existing order. This is an illustrative workflow, not a deployed benchmark.

The host first establishes the operator's permitted warehouse and order scope. It selects the reservation capability only after resolving the exact part identifier and checking relevant order evidence. The integration sends a bounded request with a stable logical action identity.

With a direct adapter, application code translates that request into the service's HTTP contract. With an MCP adapter, the host issues the appropriate tool invocation and the server translates it into the same business request. Neither path should allow the model to invent warehouse authority.

Suppose the inventory service commits the reservation, but the response is lost. An extra protocol layer does not determine whether the reservation happened. Both adapters need to reconcile by the logical action identifier and return an explicit unknown or pending outcome while evidence is incomplete.

HTTP's definition of idempotence concerns the intended effect of repeated requests, and it cautions against automatic retry of non-idempotent requests without an appropriate basis. Choosing a transport does not establish safe repetition for a business mutation. [RFC 9110, idempotent methods](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-idempotent-methods).

Once the reservation is confirmed, the final answer should identify the authoritative reservation result. A successful protocol exchange, a valid JSON object, and a completed inventory reservation are three separate claims. See [idempotency for agent actions](/blog/idempotency-ai-agent-actions) for the shared action-ledger design.

## Compare the operational costs explicitly

Use a decision table tied to the actual product:

| Question | Direct adapter can fit | MCP can earn its cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who consumes the capability? | One controlled application | Several compatible agent hosts |
| How does the catalog change? | Small, intentionally fixed interface | Reusable discoverable capability surface |
| Who owns compatibility? | One application team | Multiple clients and server owners |
| What already exists? | Mature API and adapter infrastructure | Repeated host-specific integration work |

These are proposed decision criteria, not measured performance results. A protocol choice should not be justified by an assumed universal latency advantage. Measure complete task latency, including initialization, authorization, downstream work, result validation, and recovery.

Also account for ownership. An MCP server needs deployments, dependency updates, supported-client testing, and an on-call path. A direct adapter needs equivalent attention to its own service contract. Reusing an existing operationally mature service can be more valuable than standardizing a thin layer that nobody owns after launch.

## Validate behavior across both boundaries

Create contract fixtures for valid arguments, missing fields, stale resource versions, unauthorized tenants, pending results, and unknown outcomes. Assert the business effect as well as the returned text. Three reserved units should remain three after a lost response and retry, rather than quietly becoming six.

For MCP, add unsupported-version negotiation, unavailable advertised capabilities, malformed structured results, reconnects, and changed tool catalogs. For direct HTTP, add unexpected status codes, incompatible response bodies, and server-side validation changes. Neither adapter should silently reinterpret a changed response as success.

Then run representative agent tasks against both variants with the same evidence, permissions, acceptance criteria, and downstream service behavior. Compare accepted outcomes, diagnosis time, recovery behavior, and operational effort. The result may justify using both: a stable business API as the authority and an MCP surface for hosts that benefit from that protocol.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does MCP replace an existing REST API?

It can expose a capability interface in front of that API. The business service can remain the system of record, with the MCP server handling protocol translation and host-facing contracts.

### Is an OpenAPI-generated tool catalog sufficient?

It can provide useful structural information, but the catalog still needs review for task relevance, authority, ambiguity, and recovery semantics. Generating a schema does not decide which operations an agent should possess.

### Does MCP make a tool call safe automatically?

No. Safe execution still depends on authenticated scope, current-state checks, action identity, result verification, and enforced business rules. Protocol conformance and authorization correctness require separate evidence.
researchNote: Read the versioned MCP architecture, tools, lifecycle and authorization specifications, OpenAPI 3.1.1, and RFC 9110 on 2026-11-10. Explicit versions are cited without claiming they are the latest releases. The inventory design and comparison criteria are illustrative, not a deployed implementation or benchmark. Source summaries are limited; most prose develops independent engineering reasoning.
